checks.explanation: Small ambient integral error need not give small error on a finite set of graph encodings, or on a graph distribution supported there. Acknowledging possible mislabelling does not supply a relation between the approximation norm and the graph error. checks.demonstration: Fix finitely many distinct graph encodings \(z_1,\ldots,z_K\) in the ambient tensor space. Around each encoding choose a continuous bump of height one and support radius \(\delta\). Their sum has value one at every encoding, while its \(L^p\) norm tends to zero as \(\delta\to0\), because the total support volume tends to zero. Thus an arbitrarily small ambient \(L^p\) error can coexist with a fixed error on every graph in that finite set. This demonstrates the missing norm-to-data bridge; it is not a construction proving that no Transformer can classify the graphs. Separately, with \(M:X\to Y\), \(f:Y\to Y\), and \(S:Y\to Z\), the compatible composition is \(S\circ f\circ M:X\to Z\).
checks.repair: Correct the composition to \(S\circ f\circ M\). To justify classification, supply a uniform approximation result on the graph-encoding set with error smaller than the label margin, or an approximation theorem in the graph-data measure. For a finite set with atomic weights \(w_j\ge w_{\min}>0\), an \(L^p\) error at most \(\varepsilon\) under that measure implies \(\|f(z_j)-g(z_j)\|\le\varepsilon w_{\min}^{-1/p}\) at every encoding. Choosing this below the classification margin proves the desired finite-set conclusion. The cited ambient Lebesgue theorem does not provide either of these replacements; their applicability to the proposed architecture needs to be established.
checks.scope: A gap in the reduction from approximation to graph discrimination, plus a local composition-order error. Full-eigenpair reconstruction remains valid, and the source’s explicit approximate-solution qualification is retained. No impossibility theorem for SAN is claimed.

$$S_m=2\left(c_0+c_1+2\log_2(m/2)\right)=O(\log m).$$

Let $N_m=\binom{m-4}{(m-4)/2}$. There are $N_m^2$ distinct members. For each fixed auxiliary input $m$, fewer than $2^L$ programs have length below $L$. Taking $L=\lfloor2\log_2N_m\rfloor$, at least one member satisfies

$$K(W_m\mid m)\ge\lfloor2\log_2N_m\rfloor=2m-O(\log m).$$

The shape and precision are computable from $m$ and the fixed construction, so supplying them changes this conclusion by at most a constant. Also $K(W_m)\ge K(W_m\mid m)-O(1)$. Neither a universal additive constant nor an $O(\log m)$ shape or self-delimiting header bridges the linear gap between $K$ and $S_m$. The argument requires neither numerical CTM entries nor the exact complexity of a particular finite matrix.

Plane independence does not supply the missing order information. The tails can be sampled independently and uniformly from their balanced-sequence class. Choose a pair with joint conditional complexity at least $2\log_2N_m-O(1)$ given $m$. Each tail has a fixed-length enumeration code of length $\lceil\log_2N_m\rceil$ once $m$ is supplied. The prefix-complexity concatenation inequality then gives

$$K(u_{\rm tail}\mid v_{\rm tail},m)\ge\log_2N_m-O(1),\qquad
K(v_{\rm tail}\mid u_{\rm tail},m)\ge\log_2N_m-O(1).$$

Consequently the directed algorithmic mutual information between tails conditional on $m$ is at most a constant. Without conditioning, describing their common size costs at most $O(\log m)$. The fixed anchors add no growing information. Independence of successive blocks is an assumption of the separate saturation Proposition 3.3, not a hypothesis attached to the claimed upper bound. This construction does not invoke the saturation formula.

Appendix A's discussion of exact ordered block descriptions does not add an order code to Equation (2). The public qbdm.py calls BDM on each plane and adds its scores; its optional blockwise quantizer changes local ranges, not the score into a partition-tree code. The default global quantizer is lossless on this family. The documented PyBDM aggregation likewise adds only a CTM value and logarithmic multiplicity. The original BDM paper already gives this limitation: Figure 4 discusses equal scores under block permutations, and Section 4.3, Proposition 1 includes an arrangement-dependent $O((\log |A|)^2)$ correction and CTM approximation error in its upper comparison with $K$, where $A$ denotes possible arrangements. The present construction applies that known distinction to QuBD; it does not claim a new limitation of BDM.

Enumerating all 36 anchored pairs at $m=8$ verifies identical histograms and exact quantization, and decodes each pair from its ranks. This finite enumeration illustrates the construction; the counting argument proves the asymptotic separation. The paper's saturation and partition-dependence qualifications are consistent with treating the score as a structural statistic, but do not establish its universal upper-bound interpretation.
checks.repair:
Remove the universal upper-bound interpretation of the finite score and describe it as a structural statistic. Separate the exact retained-bit residual argument from any claim about substituting a CTM/BDM score for $K$. This leaves the reported statistic and empirical comparisons intact while withdrawing the unsupported estimator guarantee. Claims of strict residual improvement elsewhere in the paper require separate arguments.

A genuine description-length upper bound requires a decoder. Encode the shape and precision, a dictionary of literal blocks or verified decodable block programs, the multiplicities, and the block order. With $m$ blocks and multiplicities $n_w$, there are $m!/\prod_w n_w!$ orders of that multiset. A rank among them uses $\lceil\log_2(m!/\prod_w n_w!)\rceil$ bits. The preceding metadata must be self-delimiting, so the decoder knows each field and the rank length. Treating a CTM-table number as the length of an available program is insufficient.

If this prefix-decodable representation has length $L(W)$, a fixed interpreter gives $K(W)\le L(W)+O(1)$. For the counterfamily, a self-delimiting encoding of $m$ followed by two fixed-length tail ranks has length $2\log_2N_m+O(\log m)$ and reconstructs every member. The order cost is linear in $m$; the header cost is logarithmic. This is a different score and does not prove that the original score is a tighter bound than BDM.
checks.scope: The finding concerns the universal upper-bound and finite-estimation-error interpretation of the computed score $S(W)$. The missing block-order cost is already recognized in the original BDM literature. QuBD itself acknowledges saturation, partition dependence and possible dependence between bit-planes. Its exact-complexity residual identities and its computed empirical comparisons are not refuted by this objection. A sufficient repair is to present $S$ as a structural statistic and restrict theoretical claims to the information retained by the representation.

checks.location: utils/ptq_utils.py:80–93; ptq.py:11,99–110
checks.explanation: At $b=1$, the scale denominator is zero. A nonzero finite channel therefore obtains an infinite scale, and reconstructing its rounded zero codes multiplies zero by infinity, producing NaNs. At other supported precisions an all-zero channel gives scale zero and divides zero by zero. The one-bit case is inside the published sweep.
checks.demonstration:
The source rule is $s_c=a_c/(2^{b-1}-1)$ followed by $Q_b(x_{c,i})=\operatorname{round}(x_{c,i}/s_c)s_c$. For a finite channel with $a_c>0$ and $b=1$, IEEE arithmetic gives

$$2^{b-1}-1=0,\qquad s_c=+\infty,\qquad x_{c,i}/s_c=0,\qquad Q_1(x_{c,i})=0\cdot\infty=\mathrm{NaN}.$$

If $a_c=0$, then $s_c=0$ at $b\geq2$ and $x_{c,i}/s_c=0/0$ is already NaN. The source has separate branches for four-dimensional weights, two-dimensional weights and other shapes; each uses the same denominator and unguarded reconstruction.

The unchanged forward function was extracted from pinned source and evaluated with a float32 NumPy tensor-arithmetic adapter. Nonzero arrays of shapes $(2,4)$, $(2,2,2,2)$ and $(4,)$ produced only NaNs at one bit and finite outputs at two and eight bits. Zero arrays produced NaNs at two bits. The adapter preserves the reductions, broadcasting and nearest-even rounding used by these cases. These arithmetic results come from the float32 NumPy adapter; native Torch behavior was not tested.

The current helper and script are byte-identical to the inspected May commit. The script actually installs this quantizer on model weights and enables it; an unused helper or an unsupported bit width cannot explain away the path. No ImageNet evaluation was run, and these calculations do not establish which code generated Figure 7.
checks.repair:
Restrict this quantizer's advertised sweep to integer widths $b\in\{2,\ldots,8\}$ and reject $b=1$. If a one-bit result is retained, define a separate binary quantizer and evaluate it. The defective function cannot support a one-bit result; establishing the provenance of Figure 7 requires the actual evaluation code and outputs.

For the remaining widths, handle zero scales explicitly. With $s_c=a_c/(2^{b-1}-1)$, set $\widetilde s_c=1$ when $s_c=0$ and $\widetilde s_c=s_c$ otherwise, then compute

$$Q_b(x_{c,i})=\operatorname{round}(x_{c,i}/\widetilde s_c)s_c.$$

An all-zero channel returns zero without division by zero. For a nonzero representable scale, this is exactly the existing rule. Under the float32 NumPy adapter, the modified function rejects unsupported one-bit input, preserves the tested nonzero two- and eight-bit outputs, and returns zero for zero channels. Native Torch behavior and model-level results require a new evaluation with the corrected supported domain.

checks.location: App. C.4, proof of Theorem 4 (Eq. 18); main-text Eq. 9
checks.claim: Theorem 4: ||phi(F^L) - phi(hat F)|| <= sum_{t in T} ||J_{:,t}(hat F)||_F ||rho_t|| + beta/2 sum_{t in T} ||rho_t||^2, proved using that kept tokens are unchanged by pruning.
checks.explanation: The proof asserts that kept tokens have exactly the same final features in both runs. Pruning before later self-attention blocks can change those features, even when the pruned tokens are restored before the final block. The Taylor expansion then contains kept-token contributions that the displayed bound omits.
checks.demonstration:
Start with two tokens of width two, with features $e=(1,-1)$ and $0$. Use a residual self-attention block with zero queries and keys, identity value and output maps, and a scaled LayerNorm $n$ satisfying $n(e)=e$ and $n(0)=0$. Such a LayerNorm is obtained with normalization constant $1$, gain $\sqrt2$ and zero bias. Both tokens receive the average value $e/2$, so the unpruned block outputs $(3e/2,e/2)$.

Now freeze and remove token $1$. The remaining zero token stays zero through the same block. Restore the frozen token before a final identity block. The final tensors are therefore

$$F^L=\begin{pmatrix}3/2&-3/2\\1/2&-1/2\end{pmatrix},\qquad\hat F=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}.$$

Here $\mathcal T=\{1\}$, the fusion correction is $\Delta_1=0$, and the removed-token residual is $\rho_1=e/2$. Choose the linear decoder $\phi(F)=F_{2,1}$. Its Hessian is zero and its Jacobian block for token $1$ is zero. The claimed bound is thus zero, whereas

$$|\phi(F^L)-\phi(\hat F)|=\frac12.$$

The output error comes entirely from token $2$, which was kept. The final identity block is a valid residual block with zero attention and MLP branches.
checks.repair:
Include the actual final residual of every token, $E_t=F_t^L-\hat F_t$. Taylor’s integral remainder and the triangle inequality give

$$\|\phi(F^L)-\phi(\hat F)\|_2\le\sum_{t=1}^{N}\|J_{:,t}(\hat F)\|_F\|E_t\|_2+\frac\beta2\sum_{t=1}^{N}\|E_t\|_2^2.$$

Here the second-derivative bound means $\|D^2\phi(Z)[U,U]\|_2\le\beta\|U\|_F^2$ along the segment. The first-order term decomposes over all token blocks, and the integral remainder is at most $\beta\|F^L-\hat F\|_F^2/2$. On removed tokens, $E_t=\rho_t$; the added terms account for changes to kept tokens.

This proves a corrected decoder-error bound. To justify choosing a pruning set from removed-token importance alone, one must also control the kept-token residuals and the dependence of the Jacobian on that set. No such control is provided by the stated hypotheses. Alternatively, the original restricted sum is valid if the theorem explicitly assumes $E_t=0$ on every kept token; the described attention pipeline does not guarantee that condition.
checks.scope: This concerns the removed-token-only bound in Theorem 4 and Equations (9) and (18), and its use to justify the selection criterion in Corollary 3. The full-residual correction bounds decoder error but does not restore that selection guarantee.
checks.claimContext: Theorem 4 and Equation (9) compare a decoder’s outputs at the final feature tensors $F^L,\hat F\in\mathbb R^{N\times D}$, obtained without and with pruning followed by Last-Layer Fusion. For the removed set $\mathcal T$, write $\rho_t=F_t^L-F_t^\ell-\Delta_t$, where $F_t^\ell$ is token $t$’s feature when it is frozen and $\Delta_t$ is its fusion correction. The decoder $\phi$ is twice continuously differentiable, $J_{:,t}(\hat F)$ is its Jacobian block for token $t$, and $\beta$ bounds its second derivative along the segment between the final tensors. The claimed bound sums only over removed tokens.
checks.whyItMatters: Decoder error can come entirely from a kept token, while the bound’s removed-token contribution is zero. Adding the missing terms repairs the Taylor inequality but leaves the proposed importance-based selection rule without this guarantee.
checks.title: The pruning bound omits changes to kept-token features
checks.verificationNote: The theorem’s written assumptions do not require kept-token invariance. Such invariance is sufficient for the original formula, but is not implied by running later attention blocks on a reduced token set.
checks.checkedLocation: Appendix C.4, Theorem 4 and Equation (18); Section 7, Equation (9), and the hard-pruning/last-layer-fusion definition

checks.location: Section 3.2 Proposition 1, Eq. (7), text line 140; proof Section D.1, text line 1781
checks.claim: The unweighted DDPM simple-loss sum is an upper bound on the negative log-likelihood of the composed model, hence minimising one term of it is 'directionally aligned' with maximising the log-density.
checks.explanation: The DDPM variational bound includes schedule-dependent weights, a terminal prior term and a reconstruction term. Replacing it by an unweighted sum does not preserve the displayed inequality. Training the denoiser with the standard DDPM objective does not make those terms disappear. Also, being one nonnegative summand of an upper bound would not by itself prove that reducing a single probe loss increases the model density.
checks.demonstration: Use one local model and data $x_0\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$. Let $T=2$, $\beta_1=0.01$, $\beta_2=0.10$, and write $a_s=\prod_{j=1}^s(1-\beta_j)$, so $a_1=0.99$ and $a_2=0.891$. The exact DDPM-optimal denoiser is $\epsilon_\theta(x_s,s)=\sqrt{1-a_s}\,x_s$. For a fixed clean input $x$, its error is $a_s^2+a_s(1-a_s)x^2$. Thus $L_{\mathrm{simple}}(x)=1.773981+0.107019x^2$. Choose the standard Gaussian reverse kernels with variance $\beta_s$ and the corresponding DDPM mean $\sqrt{1-\beta_s}\,x_s$. Starting from variance one, the recursion $v_{s-1}=(1-\beta_s)v_s+\beta_s$ gives $v_0=1$, hence $p_\theta=\mathcal N(0,1)$. At $x=10$, the printed left side is $12.475881$, whereas $-\log p_\theta(10)=50+\tfrac12\log(2\pi)\approx50.918939$. The quadratic coefficients also show that no additive constant independent of $x$ repairs this example.
checks.repair: For a specified forward chain $q$ and normalized reverse kernels $p_\theta$, use the negative evidence lower bound $\mathcal B(x)=\mathbb E_{q(x_{1:T}\mid x)}[\log q(x_{1:T}\mid x)-\log p_\theta(x_{0:T})]$. Whenever these quantities are finite, $\mathcal B(x)=-\log p_\theta(x)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q(x_{1:T}\mid x)\|p_\theta(x_{1:T}\mid x))\ge-\log p_\theta(x)$. Its DDPM expansion retains the terminal KL, reverse-step KL terms and reconstruction likelihood, including all variance-dependent weights and constants. The reconstruction-to-noise-error equality may still motivate a surrogate objective, but a guarantee about its guidance direction needs a separate argument relating its gradient to the density gradient.
checks.scope: This refutes Proposition 1's unrestricted inequality in arXiv v2, uploaded October 10, 2026, even with an exact denoiser and no composition ambiguity. The two-step example does not establish failure under the paper's longer experimental schedule, and validity for a particular Gaussian long-schedule example would not establish the general proposition. It does not assess the reported planning results.
checks.whyItMatters: The density interpretation of reconstruction guidance requires the actual variational bound, including the terms omitted from the printed inequality.
checks.title: The unweighted denoising loss is not the claimed likelihood upper bound
checks.claimContext: Proposition 1 identifies a weighted reconstruction error with the sum of DDPM noise-prediction errors, then claims this sum upper-bounds the negative log-likelihood of the composed reverse model. Appendix D.1 acknowledges a timestep reweighting, but the proposition prints the unweighted sum itself as the bound. The equality between reconstruction and noise-prediction errors is valid.

checks.location: Section D.3 Proposition 3, text lines 1823-1861 (Eq. 24 line 1846, Eq. 25 line 1852, key step line 1856)
checks.claim: Adding the time-independent score correction -w grad E_RCD makes the guided reverse process have marginals p_t * exp(-w E_RCD), so the sampler targets that tilted distribution exactly.
checks.explanation: The score of the proposed density is indeed $\nabla\log p_t-w\nabla E$. That algebraic identity does not establish that the family of proposed densities satisfies the diffusion’s evolution equation or its initial condition. A fixed energy tilt at every noise level generally differs from the time-dependent tilt induced by weighting the final samples.
checks.demonstration:
Take two overlapping segments, $(x_1,x_2)$ and $(x_2,x_3)$, with standard Gaussian local densities. Their exact scores agree on the overlap, so arithmetic score averaging gives the composed density $p_0=\mathcal N(0,I_3)$.

At probe level $\alpha_s=1/2$, the exact local Tweedie reconstructions also agree on the shared coordinate. Merging them gives $x^{\mathrm{rec}}=(x+\epsilon)/2$, where $\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I_3)$. Thus the overlap penalty is zero and the paper's reconstruction energy is

$$E_{\mathrm{RCD}}(x)=\mathbb E\|x-x^{\mathrm{rec}}\|^2=\frac14\|x\|^2+\frac34.$$

Use the stationary forward diffusion $dX_t=-X_t\,dt+\sqrt2\,dW_t$. Its marginals remain $\mathcal N(0,I_3)$. With guidance weight $w=2$, the claimed energy tilt has covariance $I_3/2$ at every noise level. But each coordinate's forward variance obeys $v'=2-2v$, which equals $1$ at $v=1/2$. The claimed constant tilted family therefore fails the forward evolution equation.

There is also a direct endpoint calculation. The proposed modified score is $-2x$, so in increasing reverse time $u$ the SDE becomes

$$dY_u=-3Y_u\,du+\sqrt2\,dB_u.$$

Each coordinate's variance satisfies

$$v(u)=\frac13+\left(v(0)-\frac13\right)e^{-6u}.$$

Starting from the original Gaussian noise gives $v(1)\approx0.335$, rather than the claimed $1/2$. Starting from the proposed tilted noise with $v(0)=1/2$ also fails to preserve that constant variance. This uses the actual expected reconstruction energy of overlapping Gaussian segments, rather than an arbitrary external energy.
checks.repair:
For an exact endpoint tilt, propagate its weight through the reference forward diffusion. Let $E$ denote the terminal reconstruction energy and define

$$h_t(x)=\mathbb E[e^{-wE(X_0)}\mid X_t=x],\qquad q_t(x)=\frac{p_t(x)h_t(x)}Z,$$

where $Z=\mathbb E[e^{-wE(X_0)}]$. The required score is $\nabla\log p_t+\nabla\log h_t$, and the reverse process must start from $q_T$.

For the Gaussian example above, the correctly propagated tilted covariance is

$$v_t I_3,\qquad v_t=1-\frac12e^{-2t}.$$

The required score is $-x/v_t$, so the correction to the reference score is

$$\nabla\log h_t(x)=-\frac{e^{-2t}}{2-e^{-2t}}\,x.$$

Its reverse-time variance equation follows $v_{T-u}$ and ends at $1/2$ in each coordinate. This provides an exact correction when the conditional expectation and the matching noise-end distribution are available. Keeping the paper's existing guidance instead requires describing it as energy-guided sampling without asserting this exact endpoint density.
checks.scope: The error concerns the exact distributional interpretation in Proposition 3's idealized SDE. Its statement and proof are unchanged between public v1 and v2, uploaded May 4 and October 10, 2026. The implemented normalized gradient through a clean-sample estimate is a different vector field and is not proved exact by that SDE argument. The conditional-potential correction changes both guidance and reverse initialization; the reported planning measurements are separate empirical claims.
checks.whyItMatters: A guidance field can improve generated plans without sampling an exact specified density. The endpoint-law claim requires a compatible evolution and initialization, not just the correct score for a proposed density.
checks.title: Static energy guidance does not give the claimed Gibbs endpoint law
checks.claimContext: Appendix D.3, Proposition 3, adds the score correction $-w\nabla E(x)$ to a reverse diffusion and claims that its time marginals are $q_t(x)\propto p_t(x)e^{-wE(x)}$, hence that its endpoint has the same energy tilt. Here $p_t$ is the unguided marginal density, $E$ is the RCD reconstruction energy and $w>0$ is the guidance weight.

review-neurips-2026-149803.title: Stochastic Grouping Conformal Prediction for Effective Subgroup Reliability

checks.location: Proposition3; proof deferred to unavailable AppendixA.3
checks.claim: Exchangeability and continuous marginal transformed score suffice for subgroup coverage>=1−alpha−DeltaG.
checks.explanation: Under exchangeability, the calibration cutoff can depend on which subgroup the test point belongs to. Matching the subgroup and marginal score distributions does not control this dependence.
checks.demonstration:
Use one calibration example, one test example and $\alpha=1/2$. Draw $U$ uniformly on $[0,1)$ and form the two records
$$ (A,U),\qquad (B,(U+1/4)\bmod1),$$
where the first coordinate is a group and the second is a score. Uniformly permute the records into calibration and test positions. The pair is exchangeable, and each group's score is uniform, so $\Delta_B=0$.

The cutoff is the single calibration score. Conditional on the test record belonging to $B$, it is covered exactly when $(U+1/4)\bmod1\leq U$, which occurs with probability $1/4$. The proposition instead gives a lower bound of $1/2$. These are valid classification scores: take true label one, classifier probabilities $(1-v,v)$ at a record with score $v$, and a fixed identity-CDF transform.
checks.repair:
Condition on the independently fitted score law and require iid calibration/test observations, or explicitly impose the needed independence between the cutoff and the test score/group. Let $F$ and $F_G$ be the resulting fixed marginal and subgroup score CDFs. For every cutoff $q$,
$$F_G(q)\geq F(q)-\Delta_G.$$
If $k=\lceil(m+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil\leq m$, continuity gives $\mathbb E F(V_{(k)})=k/(m+1)\geq1-\alpha$; the fallback cutoff covers all scores. Taking expectations proves the stated bound under these hypotheses. If fitting randomness is averaged over, use the conditional discrepancy's expectation or a uniform bound on it.
checks.scope: This is a failure of the exchangeability-only subgroup assertion. Marginal conformal validity is consistent with the counterexample. An iid statement conditional on the fitted transform has the sufficient repair above.
checks.title: The subgroup bound needs more than exchangeability
checks.claimContext: Proposition 3 assumes split-conformal exchangeability and continuous transformed scores. It bounds subgroup coverage using the Kolmogorov distance $\Delta_G$ between subgroup and marginal score distributions. The calibration set is separated from training; calibration/test independence is not stated in the proposition.

Substituting \(r_{\mathrm{side}}\) gives \(\alpha/2\) for each endpoint. Substituting \(r_{\mathrm{alg}}\) gives \(\alpha/2+1/[2(N_c+1)]\), so adding the two bounds gives \(\alpha+1/(N_c+1)\). For example, \(N_c=99\) and \(\alpha=0.1\) give targets \(4/99\) and \(1/22\), respectively; the resulting total expectation bounds are \(0.10\) and \(0.11\).

checks.scope: This establishes a formula inconsistency and the extra slack in the stated finite-sample calculation. It does not establish that a measured coverage rate exceeds its target. Correcting the budget does not replace the monotonicity and selection conditions required by the calibration theorem.

We conduct an ablation study to verify the effectiveness of each component in the dual-conditioning framework, as summarized in Table 4. In the table, Str. Cond. and Sem. Cond. denote structural condition and semantic condition, respectively. checks.location: Assumption 3.1(a), lines 189-193; Appendix B Terms III-IV, lines 1370-1383 and 1424-1453

checks.explanation: Regularity in one coordinate supplies no regularity in the other. A bounded loss can be Lipschitz in predictions and discontinuous in responses.
checks.demonstration:
Let \(c(z)=\min\{1,\max\{0,z\}\}\) and define
\[\ell(y,z)=\big(c(z)-\mathbf1\{y\ge1/2\}\big)^2.\]
The loss is bounded by one. For fixed \(y\), its Lipschitz constant in \(z\) is at most two, because clipping is 1-Lipschitz and the derivative of \((t-h)^2\) on \([0,1]\), with \(h\in\{0,1\}\), has magnitude at most two. Thus Assumption 3.1(a) holds with \(B_\ell=2\).

At prediction \(z=0\), responses \(y_-=1/2-\varepsilon\) and \(y_+=1/2+\varepsilon\) have losses zero and one. Their distance is \(2\varepsilon\). No finite uniform response-Lipschitz constant follows from the printed assumption.
checks.repair:
Add the separate response condition
\[|\ell(y,z)-\ell(y',z)|\le L_y|y-y'|\]
on the relevant response and prediction ranges. For any coupling of response laws \(P_x,Q_x\) at a fixed covariate, integration gives a loss difference at most \(L_y\mathbb E|Y-Y'|\). Taking the infimum over couplings yields \(L_yW_1(P_x,Q_x)\); averaging over the common covariate law proves the conditional risk bound.

For ordinary squared loss on \([0,1]\), the required constant is two in each coordinate, so this addition does not exclude that standard example. It repairs the regularity step but does not justify replacing a conditional transport discrepancy by a marginal one.

checks.location: Theorem 3.4; Appendix B Term III, conditional-to-marginal Wasserstein identity, line 1383
checks.claim: Marginal quantile matching controls conditional predictive risk; the theorem's transfer-bias term is the marginal W2 distance.
checks.explanation: The matching term compares unconditional response laws, but prediction risk depends on responses paired with the same covariate. Equal response marginals can hide different conditional means. The equality in Appendix B replacing an expected conditional Wasserstein distance by a marginal distance is therefore false, and zero marginal mismatch does not make source augmentation harmless.
checks.demonstration:
Use one source domain and let \(X\) be uniform on \(\{0,1,2\}\) in both domains. On \(y\in[0,1]\), define conditional densities
\[p_0(y\mid x)=1+a_x(2y-1),\qquad p_1(y\mid x)=1+b_x(2y-1),\]
where \(a=(-0.6,0,0.3)\) and \(b=(0,0.3,-0.6)\). All densities are strictly positive, the joint supports agree, and the covariate ratio is one. Both response marginals have density \(1-0.1(2y-1)\), so their marginal Wasserstein distance is zero.

Their conditional means nevertheless differ:
\[m_0(x)=\frac12+\frac{a_x}{6},\qquad m_1(x)=\frac12+\frac{b_x}{6}.\]
Take \(\mathcal F=\{m_0,m_1\}\) and squared loss on \([0,1]\), extended globally by clipping each argument to that interval. This loss is bounded by one and is \(2\)-Lipschitz in each argument. Since \(m_0\) is the target Bayes mean, its exact excess-risk identity gives
\[R(m_1)-R(m_0)=\frac13\sum_{x=0}^2\left(\frac{a_x-b_x}{6}\right)^2=\frac7{600}>0.\]
The conditional CDF difference is \((a_x-b_x)(y^2-y)\), so independently
\[\mathbb E_XW_1(P_0(\cdot\mid X),P_1(\cdot\mid X))=\frac13\sum_x\frac{|a_x-b_x|}{6}=\frac1{10}.\]
Thus the conditional discrepancy is positive before any learning calculation, while the marginal discrepancy is zero.

Use exact inverse-CDF generators, bounded by one, and exact covariate weights. The only affine marginal match is \(\beta_*=(0,1)\): preserving the support \([0,1]\) permits identity or reflection, and reflection reverses the nonzero marginal tilt. Hence \(\mathcal B\) is the bounded singleton required by the theorem. Empirical marginal matching converges to that unique minimizer: empirical means and variances keep its coefficients bounded, and quantile consistency identifies the limit.

Now take \(n_1=n_0^2\). The source portion dominates the augmented empirical loss, so its minimizer over the finite class converges to \(m_1\). Generator and weighting errors are zero, the finite-class complexity vanishes, and the empirical marginal-matching error tends to zero. Every term on the claimed right-hand side therefore vanishes, whereas target excess risk tends to \(7/600\). This is an asymptotic contradiction to the arXiv v1 guarantee, not a claim that every finite sample selects the source mean.
checks.repair:
Retain a conditional discrepancy. With a common covariate law and loss \(L\)-Lipschitz in its response argument, coupling responses at the same covariate gives
\[|R_P(f)-R_Q(f)|\le L\,\mathbb E_XW_1(P(\cdot\mid X),Q(\cdot\mid X)).\]
This proves the required risk-bias step with a conditional term. Matching response marginals alone does not make that term small, as the construction shows.

The author's [28 July 2026 code correction](https://github.com/facebookresearch/TLCQM/commit/eda8f1c7551c0c9b54c62371258a620639796ff1) replaces global marginal sorting by conditional CRPS matching within each covariate row. It preserves response–covariate pairing: in the two-row permutation example, the original global objective is zero for both aligned and swapped responses, while the conditional objective gives zero and one. This change addresses the identified pairing defect, but uses a different estimator. A full generalization theorem for that implementation needs its own assumptions and proof.

checks.location: Appendix C proof of Theorem 3.6, right-endpoint Riemann bound, lines 1711-1715
checks.claim: The quantile sum evaluated at j/n0 has quadrature error O(n0^-2) by the midpoint rule.
checks.explanation: Right-endpoint quadrature generally has a first-order error. The intended midpoint argument is recoverable here because empirical quantile functions are constant within their order-statistic bins.
checks.demonstration:
For uniform target and source distributions and \(\beta=(0,1.1)\), the squared quantile residual is \(h_\beta(u)=0.01u^2\). The identity \(\sum_{j=1}^nj^2=n(n+1)(2n+1)/6\) gives
\[\frac1n\sum_j h_\beta(j/n)-\int_0^1h_\beta(u)du=0.01\left(\frac1{2n}+\frac1{6n^2}\right).\]
Its leading order is \(n^{-1}\). At genuine midpoint indices \(c_j=(j-1/2)/n\), the error is instead \(-0.01/(12n^2)\).
checks.repair:
For the equal-size Eq. (7) idealization and the standard empirical quantile convention, \(Q_n(u)=Y_{(j)}\) on \(((j-1)/n,j/n]\). Therefore
\[\frac1n\sum_j[Q_n^Y(j/n)-Q_n^Z(j/n)]^2=\frac1n\sum_j[Q_n^Y(c_j)-Q_n^Z(c_j)]^2.\]
Rewrite the Eq. (7) empirical comparison at \(c_j\), which leaves that equal-size order-statistic objective unchanged, and compare it with the population midpoint sum. If \(h_\beta\) is twice differentiable with \(\|h_\beta''\|_\infty\le H\), the composite midpoint bound is \(H/(24n^2)\). A uniform proof over coefficients requires the same derivative bound uniformly on the coefficient region.

Alternatively, retaining the right-endpoint population grid gives the valid first-order bound \(\|h_\beta'\|_\infty/(2n)\). For literal Eq. (3), the target and generated empirical quantiles have different bin widths. Its discretization must use a common refinement or retain a valid endpoint estimate, and its additional Monte Carlo error must be controlled separately.

checks.location: Lemma C.2 quantile Hessian, lines 1512-1513 and 1553-1558
checks.claim: The quantile Hessian equals a conditional covariance term minus twice the density log-derivative times the outer product of conditional means.
checks.explanation: Adding \(\beta_0\) translates every quantile by exactly \(\beta_0\), so every Hessian entry involving the intercept must be zero. The printed density-derivative term generally makes that entry nonzero. The implicit differentiation also omits mixed derivatives.
checks.demonstration:
Let one source have density \(p(y)=2(1+y)/3\) on \([0,1]\). At \(\beta=(0,1)\) and the interior quantile \(u=1/2\),
\[q=\sqrt{5/2}-1,\qquad\frac{p'(q)}{p(q)}=\frac1{1+q}.\]
Conditioning on \(\beta^\top V=q\) determines \(V=(1,q)\), so any conditional covariance contribution vanishes. The printed intercept-intercept entry is therefore \(-2/(1+q)\ne0\).

But \(q_{(\beta_0,\beta_1)}(u)=\beta_0+q_{(0,\beta_1)}(u)\) identically. Its second intercept derivative is zero. This interior-quantile calculation does not depend on a density convention at the support endpoints.
checks.repair:
Let \(Z=\beta^\top V\), \(p(z)\) be its density, \(m(z)=\mathbb E[V\mid Z=z]\), and \(C(z)=\operatorname{Cov}(V\mid Z=z)\). Under differentiability of these conditional moments, valid differentiation of the CDF, and \(p(q)>0\), the correct formula is
\[\nabla_\beta^2 q=-\frac{\partial_z[p(z)C(z)]}{p(z)}\bigg|_{z=q}.\]
Indeed, for \(F(\beta,z)=\Pr(\beta^\top V\le z)\), differentiation gives \(F_\beta=-pm\), \(F_{\beta\beta}=\partial_z(p\mathbb E[VV^\top\mid Z=z])\), and \(q_\beta=m\). Differentiating \(F(\beta,q(\beta))=u\) twice includes both mixed terms \(F_{\beta z}m^\top\) and its transpose. Substitution cancels the mean terms, leaving \(p\nabla^2q+\partial_z(pC)=0\).

The intercept row and column of \(C\) are zero, so the corrected Hessian respects translation. Its required conditional-moment differentiability must be stated; density regularity alone does not automatically supply every derivative used here.

checks.title: The quantile Hessian violates translation in the intercept
checks.whyItMatters: A quantile derivative formula must respect exact invariances before it can support curvature calculations.

checks.location: Lemma C.4 statement and proof, lines 1627-1652
checks.claim: A deterministic empirical-objective perturbation bound follows from a supremum over x of expected absolute generator error, for every positive coefficient radius.
checks.explanation: A small expected generator discrepancy may be large on a particular noise draw. Separately, perturbing a squared loss generally has a term linear in the coefficient radius, which cannot be bounded by a quadratic-radius term uniformly as that radius approaches zero.
checks.demonstration:
Set \(n=K=C=B_g=1\), \(\beta=(0,1)\), and
\[g(u)=u,\qquad\widehat g(u)=u+\tfrac12\mathbf1\{u<10^{-3}\},\qquad U\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1].\]
Both generators lie in \([0,1]\), and \(e_1=0.0005\). At \(U=0.0005\) and target response \(Y=0.75\), the objective difference is
\[|(0.75-0.5005)^2-(0.75-0.0005)^2|=0.4995,\]
while the claimed right side is \(8\sqrt2(0.0005)<0.006\). The strict inequality persists on a neighborhood of those values, which has positive probability under independent uniform target and source draws.

For the radius defect, set \(C=0.001\), \(\beta=(0,C)\), \(g(u)=0.2+0.1u\), and \(\widehat g=g+0.1\). At \(U=0.5,Y=0.75\), the difference is \(0.00014994\), whereas the proposed bound is \(8C^2\sqrt2(0.1)\approx0.00000113\). This discrepancy is pointwise, without rare generator noise.
checks.repair:
Use empirical generator discrepancies in a deterministic bound, with \(|Y_i|\le B_g\) and the stated source-generator bounds. Put \(B=\max\{1,B_g\}\), \(D_k=n^{-1}\sum_i|\widehat g^{(k)}(X_i,\eta_i)-g^{(k)}(X_i,\eta_i)|\), and
\[A_C=2C\big(B_g+BC\sqrt{K+1}\big).\]
Bounded responses and predictions, the difference-of-squares identity, and the valid sorted-matching inequality give
\[\sup_{\|\beta\|_2\le C}|\widehat S_n(\beta)-S_n(\beta)|\le A_C\sum_kD_k.\]
To see this, each sorted prediction has magnitude at most \(BC\sqrt{K+1}\); its squared-loss change is at most \(2(B_g+BC\sqrt{K+1})\) times its displacement. Sorting does not increase total absolute matching distance, and each paired displacement is at most \(C\sum_k|\widehat g_i^{(k)}-g_i^{(k)}|\).

Conditional on fixed fitted generators and covariates, independently generated fresh noise gives \(\mathbb E D_k\le e_k\). Since each summand is at most \(2B_g\), Hoeffding and a union bound yield, with probability at least \(1-\delta\),
\[\sup_{\|\beta\|_2\le C}|\widehat S_n-S_n|\le A_C\sum_k\left(e_k+B_g\sqrt{\frac{2\log(K/\delta)}n}\right).\]
This states the sampling uncertainty and retains the necessary linear dependence on \(C\).

checks.location: Section 3.3 transfer-bias interpretation, line 256; Appendix B equation (6)
checks.claim: A target mixture of source distributions is exactly representable by an affine combination of independent source-generated responses.
checks.explanation: Convex combinations of probability laws and affine combinations of independent random variables are different operations. Convex-hull membership alone supplies no exact representation by the generator used in the paper.
checks.demonstration:
Let the covariate be constant and take independent sources with densities \(p_1(y)=2y\) and \(p_2(y)=2(1-y)\) on \([0,1]\). Their equal mixture is exactly the uniform target. All responses are bounded and there is no covariate shift.

If both affine slopes are nonzero, the resulting density is a convolution of two bounded compactly supported densities. It is continuous and tends to zero at both support endpoints, so it cannot be uniform on \([0,1]\). If only one slope is nonzero, its affine image remains triangular; if both are zero, it is a point mass. No affine coefficient vector gives an exact match.

Nor can diverging coefficients approach an unattained zero mismatch. The independent source variances are both \(1/18\), making \(\mathbb E[VV^\top]\) positive definite. Thus \(\mathbb E(\beta^\top V)^2\to\infty\) as \(\|\beta\|\to\infty\). The \(L^2\) triangle inequality for quantile functions implies \(W_2(P_0,\mathcal L(\beta^\top V))\to\infty\). This objective is continuous in \(\beta\), so it attains a strictly positive minimum. Its optimizer set is bounded, as required by Assumption 3.2(b).
checks.repair:
For zero bias in the original affine model, require the actual representability condition \(P_0=\mathcal L(\beta^\top V)\) for some admissible \(\beta\); convex-hull membership is insufficient.

To represent a conditional mixture \(P_0(\cdot\mid x)=\sum_k\pi_k(x)P_k(\cdot\mid x)\), change the generator: draw \(J\mid X=x\) with probabilities \(\pi_k(x)\), then draw \(Y=g^{(J)}(x,\eta_J)\). The law of total probability gives exactly the specified target conditional law. This is a categorical-selection model, not a correction to the coefficients of an independent affine sum.
checks.scope: Fixed in arXiv:2602.02358v2, uploaded 2 November 2026: zero transfer bias is now stated exactly when the conditional law of the calibrated response equals the target conditional law.
checks.claimContext: Section 3.3 says the transfer-bias term vanishes when the target law lies in the convex hull of the source laws. The matching model instead uses a deterministic affine combination \(\beta_0+\sum_k\beta_kY_k\) of independently generated source responses. A mixture chooses a source at random; an affine sum combines their values. Write \(V=(1,Y_1,\ldots,Y_K)^\top\).
checks.title: A distributional mixture is not an affine sum of independent responses
checks.whyItMatters: The claimed representable family determines when transfer bias can vanish. Confusing these two combinations overstates that family.
checks.verificationNote: The witness has overlapping response supports, constant covariates, bounded generators, and a bounded population optimizer set.
checks.checkedLocation: Section 3.3 convex-hull interpretation; Algorithm 1 independent source generation; Appendix B Eq. (6).

checks.location: Table 3 sparse linear predictor row, lines 1220-1224
checks.claim: Sparsity and bounded covariates alone give finite Rademacher complexity of order Bx sqrt(s log(d)/n).
checks.explanation: Sparsity limits the number of active coordinates, not the size of predictions. An unrestricted nonzero coefficient can scale the Rademacher supremum without bound.
checks.demonstration:
Take \(d=2,s=1,B_x=1\), and two observations \(X_1=X_2=(1/2,0)\). Every \(f_t(x)=t x_1\), \(t>0\), belongs to the printed class. Under the paper's absolute-value Rademacher definition, even the singleton function has
\[\frac12\mathbb E_\sigma\left|\frac t2(\sigma_1+\sigma_2)\right|=\frac t4.\]
The full class has complexity at least \(t/4\) for every \(t\), hence infinite. The strict covariate-norm restriction is satisfied.
checks.repair:
Add an explicit coefficient norm bound \(\|\Upsilon\|_2\le B_\Upsilon\), as in the adjacent nonsparse linear row. Under the printed input bound,
\[\widehat{\operatorname{Rad}}_n(\mathcal F)\le\frac{B_\Upsilon}{n}\mathbb E\left\|\sum_i\sigma_iX_i\right\|_2\le\frac{B_\Upsilon}{n}\sqrt{\sum_i\|X_i\|_2^2}\le\frac{B_\Upsilon B_x}{\sqrt n}.\]
The first inequality is Cauchy–Schwarz; the second is Jensen followed by cancellation of cross terms. Sparsity only restricts this norm-bounded class further. If a different coefficient norm is intended, state it and retain its scale in the corresponding bound.
checks.scope: Fixed in arXiv:2602.02358v2, uploaded 2 November 2026: the sparse linear class now includes the coefficient norm bound \(\|\Upsilon\|_2\le B_\gamma\).
checks.claimContext: Table 3 lists a sparse linear class with \(\|\Upsilon\|_0=s\) and \(\|x\|_2<B_x\), but places no bound on coefficient magnitude. It nevertheless gives a finite complexity rate independent of coefficient scale.
checks.title: Sparsity alone does not bound Rademacher complexity
checks.whyItMatters: A statistical complexity bound must control predictor magnitude as well as the number of selected coordinates.
checks.verificationNote: The adjacent linear row already contains a coefficient norm bound, while the sparse row omits one.
checks.checkedLocation: Table 3 sparse linear predictor row; Section 3.2 definition of empirical Rademacher complexity.

checks.location: Theorem 3.6 assumptions and Appendix C initial localization assertion, lines 288-296 and 1668
checks.claim: Bounded true/fitted generators and local curvature of the true objective suffice for localization and the stated coefficient-error rate, without generator consistency or fitted-coefficient control.
checks.explanation: Local curvature controls coefficients only after localization. Bounded outputs do not prevent a fitted generator from shrinking and a matching coefficient from diverging to undo that shrinkage.
checks.demonstration:
Take constant covariates, true target and source uniform on \([0,1]\), \(g(u)=u\), and fitted generator \(\widehat g_n(u)=u/n\). Both generators are bounded by one, while \(e_n=(1-1/n)/2\). The true optimizer set is
\[\mathcal B=\{(0,1),(1,-1)\}.\]
On the positive-slope branch the true objective Hessian is \(\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2/3\end{pmatrix}\), which is positive definite; the negative branch has the same eigenvalues. In fixed neighborhoods excluding zero slope, the projected uniform densities are positive constants on their supports. This uses the support-wise, one-sided endpoint convention for the paper's compactly supported density assumptions.

Exact population matching with the fitted generator instead requires \((0,n)\) or \((1,-n)\), at distance \(n-1\) from \(\mathcal B\). The same growth occurs with empirical target quantiles and negligible Monte Carlo error. For sorted target observations \(Y_{(i)}\) and \(c_i=(i-1/2)/n\), the positive-slope fit has
\[b_n=\frac{12}{n}\sum_iY_{(i)}(c_i-1/2),\qquad\widehat\beta_1=nb_n,\qquad\widehat\beta_0=\overline Y-b_n/2.\]
These are the exact least-squares coefficients for regressing the empirical quantile function on \(1,u\). Uniform empirical-quantile consistency gives \(b_n\to1\) and \(\widehat\beta_0\to0\), so coefficient distance grows linearly. In contrast, \(S_*=0\), the stochastic term vanishes, and \(e_n\le1/2\), making the stated right side \(O_P(1)\).
checks.repair:
A sufficient replacement is a compact coefficient domain \(\Theta\) containing \(\mathcal B\), continuity of \(S\), and uniform fitted-objective control
\[a_n=\sup_{\beta\in\Theta}|\widehat S_n(\beta)-S(\beta)|=o_P(1).\]
Let the optimizer have objective tolerance \(r_n=o_P(1)\). For every fixed neighborhood of \(\mathcal B\), assume a positive population objective gap outside it; on a compact domain this follows from continuity and \(\mathcal B\) being the complete minimizer set. The basic minimizing inequality gives
\[S(\widehat\beta)-\min_\Theta S\le2a_n+r_n,\]
so \(\widehat\beta\) enters that neighborhood with probability tending to one.

If local quadratic growth satisfies \(S(\beta)-S_*\ge c\,\operatorname{dist}_2(\beta,\mathcal B)^2\), then
\[\operatorname{dist}_1(\widehat\beta,\mathcal B)\le\sqrt{\frac{(K+1)(2a_n+r_n)}c}.\]
This proves localization and a coefficient bound under explicit hypotheses. Obtaining the paper's finer rate requires a valid uniform objective rate, consistent fitted generators, and Monte Carlo control; boundedness alone does not supply them.
checks.scope: Fixed in arXiv:2602.02358v2, uploaded 2 November 2026: the coefficient-rate theorem has been removed; the revision bounds the conditional discrepancy directly.
checks.claimContext: Theorem 3.6 bounds the distance from a fitted matching coefficient to the population optimizer set. Its assumptions bound true and fitted generators and impose local curvature on the true objective, but do not require generator consistency or a bounded fitted-coefficient search region. The proof begins by asserting that fitted minimizers eventually enter the population optimizer neighborhood. Here \(n=n_0\), \(\mathcal B=\arg\min S\), \(S_*=\min S\), and \(e_k=\sup_x\mathbb E_\eta|\widehat g^{(k)}(x,\eta)-g^{(k)}(x,\eta)|\).
checks.title: The coefficient-rate proof assumes localization without control of the fitted generators
checks.whyItMatters: A local Hessian bound cannot control an estimator that is permitted to move arbitrarily far from the region where that bound holds.
checks.verificationNote: The compact-support endpoint interpretation is stated explicitly. The witness isolates generator inconsistency and fitted-coefficient escape; no separate endpoint claim is made.
checks.checkedLocation: Theorem 3.6 and Assumptions 3.2/3.5; Appendix C opening localization assertion and subsequent coefficient-distance argument.

checks.demonstration:
The calculation is
\[\sigma^2_{\mathrm{acc}}\leq\frac14,\qquad\sigma^2_{\mathrm{cost}}\leq\frac{c_{\max}^2}{4}\]
A Bernoulli accuracy with mean \(3/4\) has variance \(3/16\), independent of the cost scale. Any sub-Gaussian variance proxy must be at least the variance, so a common proxy \(c_{\max}^2/4\) fails for sufficiently small \(c_{\max}\). The effect is not limited to proof notation: take zero costs, one query type, true model accuracies \((3/4,1/4)\), and a realizable class containing these predictions and their reversal. With one observed response per model, labels \((0,1)\) occur with probability \(1/16\) and make squared-loss ERM prefer the reversal, causing routing regret \(1/2\). A bound proportional to zero cost is then zero, and taking a positive cost upper bound arbitrarily small does not remove the mismatch.

review-neurips-2026-153642.title: Seeing Across Skies and Streets: Feedforward 3D Reconstruction from Satellite, Drone, and Ground Images

checks.location: Selected claims
checks.claim:
CrossGeo sample counts and scene splits, posed depth-acquisition pipeline and PCC filter; orthographic satellite coordinate/scale head, altitude redefinition and four-term objective.
Point-cloud and relative pose metrics, localization tables, cross-view comparisons, architectural and satellite-altitude ablations; supplementary A–G.
checks.explanation: There are no formal theorems/lemmas or a universal reconstruction/identifiability guarantee. I reconstructed the Fourier dimensions, orthographic projection and shared relative-scale gauge, training-loss terms, virtual-altitude convention, dataset counts, and the numerical comparisons underpinning the main empirical claims. A principal-point offset is naturally absorbed by centered pixel coordinates. Altitude redefinition is deliberately a virtual orthographic-camera choice; demanding unchanged pinhole intrinsics would challenge a model the authors explicitly replace. The subpixel statement lacks a relief/resolution bound. Under the paper's pinhole approximation, displacement from a ground-plane orthographic model is r*h/(H-h), yielding4.479204pixels at100m relief andthe stated300m/504px resolution. This is a conditional stress test, not measurement of any specific retained scene. Relief100m is not established for a particular source tile; reference-plane choice and orthorectification can change the residual. Therefore the screening concern remains unclear and is not manufactured into a confirmed dataset-error finding. The altitude ablation explicitly evaluates100/150/200m onthetest set, but the chronology of150m selection is not supplied. A validation-first choice followed by retrospective ablation repairs the concern without changing results; no evidence excludes that chronology. I retain the access gap rather than assert test leakage. Isolated3736/3726 count slips, opposite pitch descriptions, and every-metric ablation rhetoric were not padded into findings. The substantive comparisons checked above are not refuted by this check. Remaining gaps: No pinned public code, evaluation predictions, dataset download, GPU retraining, or benchmark rerun was available in the allowed sources. No accepted-body equivalence, public revision/erratum search, or independent second-reviewer confirmation; local-source pass only. Actual tile relief/orthorectification residuals and altitude-selection chronology remain unknown. Some prompts, figures and equations are represented only by empty/arrow placeholders in text; those image-only contents were not inspected. The full text was read.

It is worth noting that, for materials scientists, formation energy is not the most useful property to minimize since it doesn’t translate to any extravagant physical behavior.

Note also that these target properties, coming from ML oracles, introduce a synthetic bias into our model’s training.
While this may weaken the physical relevance of materials we discover, optimization of these properties provides a valid test for MBO methods in the CMD space.
In the following subsections, we evaluate CliqueFlowmer for such abilities and investigate the material representations it learned.

Qrita on CUDA and Other Hardware: 
We use Triton Tillet et al. (2019) to implement Qrita for its reduced implementation complexity and rapid prototyping capabilities. However, Triton does not guarantee maximum performance gains as it does not offer finer control over hardware resources, such as shared memory use or warp-level primitives. As such, we expect a lower-level implementation of Qrita using CUDA to provide even greater speedup over our Triton implementation. Following LatentHOI [19], physical plausibility is a heuristic, per-sequence binary score.
